nodes.label: Spreading Production Across Countries
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: MNCs divide production into small parts spread globally. Example: design in US, components in China, assembly in Mexico/Eastern Europe, customer care in India -- saving 50-60% costs. Methods: joint ventures with local companies, using local suppliers, buying local companies, placing orders with small producers.

nodes.label: Human Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Broader than human capital. Based on the idea that education and health are integral to human well-being -- not just means to productivity. Treats human beings as ends in themselves. Basic education and health are important irrespective of their contribution to labour productivity. Every individual has a right to be literate and healthy.

nodes.label: Sustainable Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Development that meets needs of present generation without compromising ability of future generations to meet their own needs (UNCED/Brundtland Commission definition). Key phrases: 'needs' (linked to resource distribution, moral issue) and 'future generations' (intergenerational equity). Edward Barbier defined it as increasing material standard of living of the poor.

nodes.label: World Trade Organisation (WTO)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: International organisation aiming to liberalise trade. Started at initiative of developed countries. Establishes rules for international trade and enforces compliance. 149 member countries (2006). Criticism: forces developing countries to remove barriers while developed countries retain protections, especially in agriculture.

nodes.label: Public Facilities
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Goods and services best provided collectively: health, education, security, PDS. Kerala's low IMR due to adequate public health and education provision. In Tamil Nadu, 75% of rural people use ration shops vs 8% in Jharkhand. Government responsibility for equitable provision.

nodes.label: Per Capita Income
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Total income of a country divided by total population (average income). World Bank criterion: countries with per capita income of Rs 4,53,000+ (2004) are rich/developed; Rs 37,000 or less are low-income countries. India was Rs 28,000 (2004) -- categorised as low-income.

nodes.label: National Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Must consider differing and conflicting notions of progress. Should an idea benefit a large number of people or only a small group? Involves thinking about fair and just paths for all. Not just about aggregate growth but equitable distribution.

nodes.label: Limitations of Average Income
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: While useful for comparison, averages hide disparities. Two countries with identical average income can have vastly different income distributions. One may have equitable distribution while another has extreme inequality. Hence, average income alone is inadequate.

nodes.label: Income and Other Goals
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: People seek not just income but also equal treatment, freedom, security, respect. Material goods alone are insufficient. Quality of life depends on non-material things like friendships, dignity, and pollution-free environment. Money cannot buy all necessary goods and services.

nodes.label: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Number of children dying before age 1 per 1000 live births in a year. Kerala: 11, Punjab: 49, Bihar: 60 (2003 data). Kerala's low IMR despite lower per capita income than Punjab demonstrates that income alone is inadequate for measuring development.

nodes.label: Literacy Rate
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Proportion of literate population in the 7+ age group. Kerala: 91%, Punjab: 70%, Bihar: 47% (2001). Significant gender disparities: in rural UP, male literacy 52% vs female 19%. Indicator of educational access and development beyond income.

nodes.label: Net Attendance Ratio
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Total children of age group 6-10 attending school as percentage of total children in same age group. Kerala: 91%, Punjab: 81%, Bihar: 41% (1995-96). More than half of children in Bihar were not in school.

nodes.label: Human Development Index (HDI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Published by UNDP in Human Development Report. Compares countries based on educational levels, health status, and per capita income. India ranked 126th out of 177 countries (2004). Sri Lanka (rank 93) ahead despite similar region. Makes clear that development is about what happens to citizens.

nodes.label: Life Expectancy at Birth
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Average expected length of life at time of birth. Sri Lanka: 74, India: 64, Pakistan: 63, Nepal: 62, Bangladesh: 63 (2004 data). Used as a health indicator in HDI alongside per capita income and education levels.

nodes.label: Sustainability of Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Present type and levels of development may not be sustainable. Resources are of two types: renewable (replenished by nature, but can be overused) and non-renewable (fixed stock, will exhaust). Groundwater overuse in 300+ districts. Crude oil reserves: 43 years at current rate globally.

nodes.label: Renewable Resources
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Resources replenished by nature -- crops, plants, groundwater (through rain). Can be overused if consumption exceeds replenishment rate. Groundwater under serious threat in many parts of India: 300 districts report 4m+ decline in 20 years. One-third of country overusing groundwater.

nodes.label: Non-Renewable Resources
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Fixed stock on earth that cannot be replenished -- crude oil, minerals, ores. Global crude oil reserves: 137 billion tonnes, lasting 43 years at current extraction. Middle East holds 89 billion tonnes. India depends on oil imports, making price increases burdensome.

nodes.label: Body Mass Index (BMI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Calculated as weight (kg) divided by square of height (metres). BMI below 18.5 indicates undernourishment; above 25 indicates overweight. Used to measure adult nutritional status. About 40% of people in India are undernourished. Not applicable to growing children.

nodes.label: Tertiary Sector (Services)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Activities that support primary and secondary sectors and provide services. Includes transport, banking, trade, communication, IT, healthcare, education. Emerged as India's largest producing sector by 2003. Production rose 11x but employment only 3x. Not all services growing equally.

nodes.label: Historical Shift Between Sectors
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Developed countries' pattern: primary dominant initially, then secondary (with industrialisation), then tertiary. In India, tertiary became largest in GDP but primary still employs most workers. This mismatch shows that enough jobs were not created in secondary and tertiary sectors.

nodes.label: Disguised Unemployment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Hidden underemployment where people appear to work but their labour contribution is less than potential. Common in agriculture where more people work on land than needed. Removing some workers would not reduce output. Also occurs in urban informal services.

nodes.label: Underemployment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: People working less than their capacity -- apparently employed but labour effort divided. Example: 5 family members on a 2-hectare plot where 3 would suffice. Removing 2 people does not affect production. Prevalent in agriculture and urban casual services.

nodes.label: Creating More Employment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Methods: irrigation investment for second crops, rural road improvement, setting up rural industries (dal mills, cold storage, honey centres), expanding education (20 lakh jobs potential) and healthcare sectors, tourism promotion (35 lakh jobs). Need both long-term and short-term measures.

nodes.label: Protection of Unorganised Sector Workers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Rural: landless labourers, small/marginal farmers (80% of rural households), sharecroppers, artisans need seeds, credit, storage, marketing. Urban: casual workers, street vendors, rag pickers. SC/ST workers face additional social discrimination. Government support essential.

nodes.label: Reasons for Tertiary Sector Growth
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Four reasons: (1) basic services like hospitals, transport, banking needed as economy develops; (2) agriculture/industry development demands supporting services; (3) rising incomes increase demand for tourism, private healthcare, education; (4) IT-based new services rapidly expanding.

nodes.label: Credit (Loans)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Agreement where lender supplies borrower with money, goods, or services for future repayment. Can have positive impact (enabling production, increasing earnings) or negative (debt trap if things go wrong). In rural areas, main demand is for crop production.

nodes.label: Terms of Credit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Comprise interest rate, collateral requirements, documentation, and mode of repayment. Vary substantially between credit arrangements depending on nature of lender and borrower. Formal sector terms generally more favourable than informal sector.

nodes.label: Collateral
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Asset owned by borrower (land, building, vehicle, livestock, bank deposits) used as guarantee until loan is repaid. If borrower fails to repay, lender can sell the collateral. Absence of collateral is a major reason preventing poor from getting bank loans.

nodes.label: Debt Trap
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Situation where credit pushes borrower into worsening cycle of debt. Occurs when loan repayment becomes impossible (e.g., crop failure) and borrower must sell assets like land. High interest rates from informal lenders make this worse -- amount to repay exceeds income.

nodes.label: Formal Sector Credit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Loans from banks and cooperatives, supervised by RBI. Banks must maintain minimum cash balance, lend to priority sectors (small cultivators, small industries, small borrowers). Meets only about half of rural credit needs. Richer households get 90% formal credit; poor households only 15%.

nodes.label: Informal Sector Credit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Loans from moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives, friends. No supervisory body. Charge much higher interest rates. Can use unfair means for recovery. Keep no records. 85% of loans to poor urban households from informal sources. Contributes to debt traps and continued poverty.

nodes.label: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Issues currency notes on behalf of central government. Supervises formal sector lending: monitors cash balances, directs lending to priority sectors (small cultivators, small industries). Banks must periodically report lending amounts, recipients, and interest rates to RBI.

nodes.label: Self Help Groups (SHGs)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Groups of 15-20 members (mainly rural women) who pool savings (Rs 25-100/month per member). Members take small loans from the group at lower rates than moneylenders. After 1-2 years of regular saving, eligible for bank loans in group's name. Overcome collateral problem. Also platform for social issues.

nodes.label: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Founded by Professor Muhammad Yunus (Nobel Peace Prize 2006). Started in 1970s, now has over 6 million borrowers in 40,000 villages. Almost all borrowers are women from poorest sections. Biggest success story in reaching the poor with credit at reasonable rates. Proved poor women are reliable borrowers.

nodes.label: Trade Barriers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Restrictions on foreign trade used by governments to regulate imports/exports. Tax on imports (tariffs) makes imported goods costlier, protecting domestic producers. Quotas limit quantity of imports. India used these post-independence to protect nascent industries in 1950s-60s. Gradually removed from 1991.

nodes.label: Globalisation Impact on Consumers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Well-off urban consumers benefit most: greater choice, improved quality, lower prices for many products. From Ambassador/Fiat era to nearly all top global car brands on Indian roads. Similar explosion of brands in electronics, clothing, food.

nodes.label: Fair Globalisation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Government must ensure globalisation benefits all, not just wealthy. Must protect small producers through infrastructure (roads, power, water), technology upgradation, and timely credit. WTO rules should be truly fair -- developed countries unfairly retain farm subsidies while forcing developing countries to open markets.

nodes.label: IT and Service Outsourcing
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Globalisation created new opportunities for Indian IT companies. Call centres, data entry, accounting, administrative tasks, engineering services done cheaply in India and exported to developed countries. Example: London magazine designed and printed in Delhi, payment via e-banking.

nodes.label: Consumer Courts (Three-Tier System)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: District level: claims up to Rs 20 lakhs. State level: Rs 20 lakhs to Rs 1 crore. National level: claims exceeding Rs 1 crore. Cases dismissed at district level can be appealed at state, then national level. Consumer can represent themselves or through consumer forums.

nodes.label: Right to Safety
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Protection against marketing of goods and services hazardous to life and property. Producers must follow required safety rules and regulations. Examples: safety valve in pressure cookers, quality of medicines. Requires both producer responsibility and government/public action to maintain quality.

nodes.label: Right to Information (Consumer)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Right to be informed about particulars of goods and services: ingredients, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date, manufacturer's address, directions for use. Enables complaints and claims for compensation if product is defective. MRP indicates maximum retail price.

nodes.label: Right to Choice
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Consumer's right to choose whether to buy a product or continue a service. Cannot be forced to buy bundled products (e.g., toothbrush with toothpaste). Right to discontinue a service. Can include right to refund if service quality is not as promised.

nodes.label: Right to Seek Redressal
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Right to seek compensation against unfair trade practices and exploitation. Compensation depends on degree of damage. Consumer forums and protection councils guide on filing cases and sometimes represent consumers in courts.

nodes.label: Maximum Retail Price (MRP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Maximum price printed on product packaging beyond which the seller cannot charge. Consumers can protest if charged above MRP. Consumers can bargain to buy at less than MRP. Part of the right to information framework protecting consumers from overcharging.

nodes.label: ISI, Agmark, and Hallmark Certification
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Quality certification logos on products. ISI: industrial products, Agmark: agricultural products (edible oil, cereals), Hallmark: jewellery. Not compulsory for all products but mandatory for those affecting health/safety or mass consumption (LPG cylinders, food colours, cement, packaged water).

nodes.label: Consumer Forums/Protection Councils
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Voluntary organisations that guide consumers on filing cases, sometimes represent them in courts. Receive financial support from government for awareness creation. Resident Welfare Associations also take up cases on behalf of members. Part of the consumer movement infrastructure.

nodes.label: Colonial Economic Policy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: British economic policies aimed at protecting and promoting British economic interests, not Indian development. India was reduced to a supplier of raw materials for British industries and a consumer of British finished goods. This two-fold exploitation systematically de-industrialised India.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: Agricultural Stagnation Under British Rule
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: About 85% of population was agrarian but productivity was extremely low. Caused by zamindari system, lack of irrigation, negligible fertiliser use, and commercialisation of agriculture forcing farmers to grow cash crops instead of food crops. Aggregate area expanded but per-hectare output stagnated.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: Zamindari System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Land revenue system under British rule, especially in Bengal Presidency. Zamindars collected rent from cultivators without investing in agricultural improvement. Revenue deposit dates were fixed, failing which zamindars lost rights, creating a cycle of exploitation of actual tillers.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: Occupational Structure Under Colonial Rule
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Agriculture accounted for 70-75% of workforce, manufacturing only 10%, services 15-20%. Little structural change occurred during colonial period. Some regional variation existed -- Madras Presidency, Maharashtra, and West Bengal saw slight decline in agricultural dependence.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: Infrastructure Under Colonial Rule
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Railways, ports, water transport, posts and telegraphs developed but primarily to serve colonial interests -- mobilising army and extracting raw materials. Roads were inadequate for rural access. Electric telegraph served law and order. Postal services remained insufficient. Real motive was not public welfare.
nodes.chapter_title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

nodes.label: IMF and World Bank Conditionalities
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India approached IBRD (World Bank) and IMF for $7 billion loan to manage the 1991 crisis. Conditions required India to liberalise and open up the economy, remove restrictions on private sector, reduce government role, and remove trade restrictions. India agreed and announced NEP.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Outsourcing
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Important outcome of globalisation where companies hire regular services from external sources, mostly from other countries. India became a major destination due to low wage rates and skilled manpower. Services outsourced include BPO/call centres, record keeping, banking, accountancy, teaching, clinical advice. Enabled by growth of IT and telecommunications.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Foreign Direct Investment and FII
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: FDI involves direct investment in productive assets by foreign entities. FII includes portfolio investment by foreign institutions (merchant bankers, mutual funds, pension funds). Post-reform, foreign investment rose from about US $100 million (1990-91) to US $150 billion (2003-04). Forex reserves grew from $6 billion to $125 billion.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Impact of Reforms on Agriculture
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Reforms have not benefited agriculture -- growth rate decelerated. Public investment in infrastructure (irrigation, power, roads, research, extension) reduced. Fertiliser subsidy removal increased costs for small farmers. WTO-driven policy changes (reduced import duties, removal of MSP, lifting of quantitative restrictions) hurt Indian farmers facing international competition.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Impact of Reforms on Industry
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Industrial growth recorded slowdown due to cheaper imports replacing domestic goods, inadequate infrastructure investment, and reduced demand. Developing countries compelled to open economies to greater flow of goods from developed countries. Indian manufacturers face competition while not getting equal access to developed country markets due to non-tariff barriers.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Service Sector Growth Post-Reforms
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Post-1991 growth concentrated in select service areas: telecommunications, IT, finance, entertainment, travel, hospitality, real estate, and trade. GDP growth increased from 5.6% (1980-91) to 6.4% (1992-2001) driven mainly by services. Vital sectors like agriculture and industry which provide livelihoods to millions did not benefit proportionally.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Fiscal Impact of Reforms
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Tax reductions did not yield larger revenue as expected. Tariff reductions curtailed customs duty revenue. Tax incentives to attract foreign investment further reduced revenue. This negatively impacted developmental and welfare expenditure. Public expenditure on social sectors was limited by reform-driven fiscal austerity.
nodes.chapter_title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal

nodes.label: Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Multi-dimensional challenge beyond just income -- includes lack of access to education, healthcare, drinking water, sanitation, housing, and political freedom. More than one-fifth of world's poor live in India. Both a call to action and a situation people want to escape. Must be defined, measured, and studied to find solutions.

nodes.label: Poverty Line
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Separates poor from non-poor. Determined by monetary value (per capita expenditure) of minimum calorie intake: 2,400 calories/day for rural and 2,100 for urban areas. In 1999-2000, poverty line was Rs 328/month (rural) and Rs 454/month (urban). Uses Monthly Per Capita Expenditure (MPCE) as proxy for income.

nodes.label: Naoroji's Poverty Line Concept
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Dadabhai Naoroji was the first in pre-independent India to discuss the concept of a poverty line. Used 'jail cost of living' as basis. Adjusted for children: assumed one-third population were children, half consumed nothing, half consumed half of adult diet, arriving at three-fourths factor for average poverty line.

nodes.label: Chronic Poor
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Category including those who are always poor and those usually poor but sometimes have slightly more (e.g., casual workers). Distinguished from transient poor (churning poor who move in and out of poverty, and occasionally poor who are usually rich but face bad patches). Non-poor are those who are never poor.

nodes.label: Head Count Ratio
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Proportion of people below the poverty line. Declined from about 55% in 1973-74 to 26% in 1999-2000. However, absolute number fell only from 321 million to 260 million. More than three-fourths of poor reside in villages. Five states (UP, Bihar, MP, West Bengal, Orissa) account for 70% of India's poor.

nodes.label: Poverty Trends in India (1973-2000)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: In 1973-74: 321 million poor (55%). In 1999-2000: 260 million poor (26%). In 1990s, absolute number of rural poor declined but urban poor increased marginally. Poverty ratio declined for both areas but gap between rural and urban remained. Gujarat reduced poverty from 48% to 15%, West Bengal from 63% to 27%.

nodes.label: Causes of Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Individual factors: low education and skills, ill health, discrimination. Structural factors: social/economic/political inequality, social exclusion, unemployment, indebtedness, unequal wealth distribution. Economy-wide: low capital formation, lack of infrastructure, population pressure, lack of welfare nets. British colonial rule substantially worsened living standards.

nodes.label: Sen Index and Alternative Poverty Measures
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Due to limitations of official poverty estimation, scholars developed alternative methods. Amartya Sen developed the Sen Index. Other tools include Poverty Gap Index and Squared Poverty Gap. These address limitations of the official method which groups all poor together and does not differentiate between very poor and other poor.

nodes.label: National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Collects consumption expenditure data used by Planning Commission to estimate official poverty data. Data collection methodology, items included in consumption basket, and poverty estimation methodology are subjects of debate among economists who question whether figures are manipulated to show reduced poverty.

nodes.label: Farmer Distress and Suicides
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Caused by: shift to commercial crops without technical support, decline in public investment in agriculture, spurious seeds/pesticides, crop failure, debt from private moneylenders at 36-120% interest, cheap imports from globalisation, lack of irrigation. Over 3,000 suicides in Andhra Pradesh, 1,000+ in Maharashtra since 2001.

nodes.label: Human Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The stock of skill and expertise embodied in people. Just as physical resources are turned into physical capital (factories), human resources (students) are turned into human capital (engineers, doctors). Treats humans as a means to increase productivity. An educated person generates more income and contributes more to economic growth than an illiterate person.

nodes.label: Sources of Human Capital Formation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Five main sources: (1) Investment in education -- individuals invest expecting higher future income, (2) Health expenditure -- increases supply of healthy labour, (3) On-the-job training -- firms train workers for enhanced productivity, (4) Migration -- people move for higher salaries despite transport/psychic costs, (5) Information -- spending to acquire labour market knowledge.

nodes.label: Human Capital vs Physical Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Physical capital is tangible, separable from owner, perfectly mobile between countries, and creates only private benefit. Human capital is intangible, inseparable from owner, not perfectly mobile (restricted by nationality/culture), and creates both private and social benefits. Both depreciate but human capital can be renewed through continuous investment.

nodes.label: Education and Economic Growth
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Educated labour contributes more to national income, stimulates innovations, and enables adaptation to new technologies. However, empirical evidence linking human capital to economic growth is nebulous due to measurement problems. Causality flows both ways: higher income builds human capital, and high human capital causes income growth.

nodes.label: Government Education Expenditure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: As percentage of GDP, increased from 0.64% (1952) to 4.02% (2002). Education Commission (1964-66) recommended 6% of GDP minimum. 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for ages 6-14. Education cess of 2% levied in 2004-05 Budget for elementary education.

nodes.label: Educational Attainment in India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Adult literacy (aged 15+): 61.9% male, 37.9% female (1990) rising to 68.4% male, 45.4% female (2000). Primary completion rate improved from 78% to 85% (male), 61% to 69% (female). Despite improvements, absolute number of illiterates equals India's population at independence. Gender gap narrowing but significant.

nodes.label: Health as Source of Human Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A sick labourer without medical access loses productivity. Health expenditure directly increases healthy labour force supply. Includes preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine, social medicine (health literacy), and provision of clean drinking water and sanitation. An important but often underestimated source of human capital formation.

nodes.label: On-the-Job Training
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Firms invest in training workers either within the firm under skilled supervision or through off-campus training. Firms insist workers stay for a specific period after training to recover the investment. Returns in enhanced productivity exceed the training costs, making it a source of human capital formation.

nodes.label: Migration as Human Capital Source
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: People migrate for higher salaries despite costs (transport, higher cost of living, psychic costs). Rural-urban migration driven by unemployment. Brain drain occurs when technically qualified persons (engineers, doctors) migrate abroad. Enhanced earnings in the new place outweigh migration costs, making it a source of human capital.

nodes.label: Gender Equity in Education
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Male-female literacy gap is narrowing (positive development) but promoting women's education remains urgent for improving economic independence, social status, and because it favourably impacts fertility rates and health care of women and children. Female literacy was only 45.4% in 2000 versus 68.4% for males.

nodes.label: Higher Education Challenges
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Indian education pyramid is steep -- fewer people reach higher education. Unemployment rate among educated youth (secondary and above) was 7.1% versus only 1.2% for those with up to primary education (NSSO data, 2000). Government needs to increase allocation and improve quality to impart employable skills.

nodes.label: Education and Health Regulatory Bodies
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Education regulated by NCERT, UGC (University Grants Commission), and AICTE (All India Council for Technical Education) at union/state levels. Health regulated by ICMR (Indian Council for Medical Research). Government intervention needed because private providers can exploit consumers who lack full information on quality and costs.

nodes.label: India as a Knowledge Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Deutsche Bank (2005) identified India as one of four major global growth centres by 2020, citing 40% expected rise in average years of education. World Bank reported India could triple per capita income by 2020 through knowledge economy transition. India has critical mass of skilled workers, functioning democracy, and diversified S&T infrastructure.

nodes.label: Self-Help Groups and Micro-Credit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Emerged to fill gaps in formal credit system where collateral requirements excluded poor rural households. Members contribute small savings, pool money, and lend to needy members at reasonable interest. By March 2003, over 7 lakh SHGs were credit-linked. SHGs empowered women but borrowings mainly for consumption, not agriculture.

nodes.label: Agricultural Diversification
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Two aspects: diversification of crop production, and shift of workforce from agriculture to allied activities (livestock, poultry, fisheries) and non-farm sectors. Necessary because depending exclusively on farming is risky, agriculture overcrowded, and seasonal unemployment during Rabi season in areas without irrigation.

nodes.label: Animal Husbandry
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Mixed crop-livestock farming system uses cattle, goats, fowl. Provides income stability, food security, transport, fuel, and nutrition without disrupting food production. Over 70 million small/marginal farmers and landless labourers find alternate livelihood. India had 287 million cattle including 90 million buffaloes (1997). Significant women employment.

nodes.label: Fisheries Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: After progressive budgetary allocations and new technologies, fisheries developed significantly. Inland sources contribute 49% and marine sector 51% of total fish production. Total fish production accounts for 1.4% of GDP. Major marine producers: Kerala, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu. Women form 60% of export marketing workforce.

nodes.label: Non-Farm Rural Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Since agriculture is overcrowded, increasing labour force needs alternate employment. Dynamic sub-sectors include agro-processing, food processing, leather industry, tourism. Traditional sectors like pottery, crafts, handlooms lack infrastructure. IT is playing critical role in rural development through info-kiosks and knowledge centres.

nodes.label: Agriculture Growth Deceleration Post-Reforms
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Agriculture sector growth decelerated to 2.3% per annum during the 1990s, lower than earlier years. Decline in public investment since 1991 identified as major reason. Inadequate infrastructure, lack of alternate employment, increasing casualisation of employment further impede rural development, leading to farmer distress across India.

nodes.label: Employment and Workers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: All persons engaged in economic activities (contributing to GNP) in any capacity are workers, including self-employed, temporarily absent, and family helpers. India had about 400 million strong workforce in 1999-2000. About three-fourths are rural workers. Men form 70% of workforce; women about 30% in rural areas but only 14% in urban areas.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Self-Employed Workers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Workers who own and operate an enterprise for their livelihood. More than half (52.6%) of India's workforce is self-employed (1999-2000). Major source of livelihood for both men (55%) and women (51%). Includes farmers, shop owners, professionals. More common in rural areas where farmers own and cultivate their own plots.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Casual Wage Labourers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Workers casually engaged in others' farms or enterprises, paid for work done. Account for 33% of India's workforce (1999-2000), more among women (37%). Most vulnerable category -- no job security, no assets, limited skills, sparse opportunities, no surplus to sustain them. Found more in rural areas.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Regular Salaried Employees
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Workers engaged by enterprises and paid wages on a regular basis. Account for only 15% of India's workforce. Men (18%) more than women (8%) due to skill requirements and higher literacy. More common in urban areas where enterprises need regular workers. Include civil engineers, bank employees, etc.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Sectoral Distribution of Workforce
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Primary sector employs 60.4% (1999-2000), down from 74.3% (1972-73). Secondary sector: 15.8%. Service/tertiary sector: 23.8%, up from 14.8%. Over 76% of rural workers in primary sector, 60% of urban workers in services. Women more concentrated in primary sector (75%) than men (54%). Shift from farm to non-farm is slow.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Formal (Organised) Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: All public sector establishments and private establishments with 10+ hired workers. Only 28 million workers (7% of 400 million) in 2001. About 20 million employed by public sector (making government the major formal employer). Only 4.8 million (17%) formal workers are women. Workers enjoy social security benefits and earn more.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Informal (Unorganised) Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: All enterprises and workers not in the formal sector -- 93% of India's 400 million workforce. Includes millions of farmers, agricultural labourers, small enterprise owners and workers, self-employed without hired workers. No regular income, no government protection or regulation, dismissed without compensation, outdated technology, no accounts maintained, workers live in slums.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Informalisation of Workforce
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Despite planned development aiming to move workers from agriculture to industry with better living standards, 93% remain in informal sector after 55 years. Reform process since 1990s actually declined formal sector employment. Employment becoming more informal with limited social security. Example: Ahmedabad textile mill closures pushed 1.3 lakh workers to informal sector.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Seasonal Unemployment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Common form in India due to agricultural seasonality. No employment opportunities in villages for all months -- work concentrated in Kharif season. Workers migrate to urban areas for jobs but return home when rainy season begins for farm work. Reflects insufficient year-round productive activities in rural areas.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Open Unemployment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: NSSO defines it as a situation where people owing to lack of work either seek work through employment exchanges, intermediaries, friends, or express willingness to work under prevailing conditions. An unemployed person is one not able to get employment of even one hour in half a day. Three data sources: Census, NSSO, and Employment Exchanges.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Government and Employment Generation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Government generates employment both directly (administrative, PSUs, hotels, transport) and indirectly (demand from government enterprises stimulates private sector employment). Multiple programmes target primary health, education, rural shelter, drinking water, nutrition, housing, road construction, wasteland development, and employment-generating assets.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Women in the Workforce
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Women account for about 30% of the workforce. Urban female participation is very low (14 per 100). Many women's activities (cooking, fetching water, farm labour) are not recognised as productive work or paid. Economists argue these women should be counted as workers. Gender discrimination in quality of employment persists across sectors.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Outsourcing and New Employment Patterns
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Newly emerging jobs mostly found in service sector. IT and outsourcing allow competitive small enterprises alongside multinationals. Home is becoming the workplace. However, this change has not favoured workers -- nature of employment has become more informal with limited social security. Government forced to take up employment generation initiatives.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: International Labour Organisation (ILO)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Through ILO's efforts, the Indian government has initiated modernisation of informal sector enterprises and provision of social security measures to informal sector workers. Plays a role in advocating for decent work conditions and worker protections globally.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Infrastructure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Support services in industrial/agricultural production, trade and commerce: roads, railways, ports, airports, dams, power stations, oil/gas pipelines, telecom, schools, hospitals, sanitation, banks. Two categories: economic (energy, transport, communication) and social (education, health, housing). India invests only 5% of GDP versus China's 20%.

nodes.label: Economic Infrastructure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Infrastructure associated with energy, transportation, and communication. Directly influences production by increasing productivity of factors of production. Includes power stations, roads, railways, ports, airports, dams, oil and gas pipelines, telecommunication facilities. Modern agriculture depends heavily on irrigation, transport, and power.

nodes.label: Social Infrastructure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Infrastructure related to education, health, and housing. Indirectly supports production by building the social sector of the economy and improving quality of life. Improvements in water supply and sanitation have large impact on reducing morbidity from waterborne diseases. Quality of transport affects access to healthcare.

nodes.label: State of Rural Infrastructure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Census 2001: only 56% of rural households had electricity, 43% still used kerosene. About 90% used bio-fuels (crop residues, dung, firewood) for cooking. Tap water available to only 24% of rural households. About 76% drank from open sources (wells, tanks, ponds). Only 6% had access to improved sanitation by 1996.

nodes.label: Energy as Infrastructure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Critical for industries, agriculture (fertilisers, pesticides, farm equipment, transportation), and households (cooking, lighting, heating). Commercial sources (coal, petroleum, electricity) account for 65% of energy consumed. Non-commercial sources (firewood, agricultural waste, dung) over 30%. More than 60% of households depend on traditional energy sources.

nodes.label: Commercial Energy Sources
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Coal (55% share), petroleum/oil (31%), natural gas (11%), hydro energy (3%). These are bought and sold, generally exhaustible (except hydro). India's critical challenge is import dependence on crude and petroleum, likely to exceed 100% in future. Oil and gas have the highest share among commercial energy consumption.

nodes.label: Non-Commercial Energy Sources
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Firewood, agricultural waste, and dried dung -- found in nature/forests, not bought and sold. Generally renewable. Over 60% of Indian households depend on these for cooking and heating. Women in rural areas walk long distances to fetch fuel and water. These are conventional but non-commercial.

nodes.label: Non-Conventional Energy Sources
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Solar energy, wind energy, and tidal power. India, being tropical, has unlimited potential for all three with appropriate cost-effective technologies. India is already the world's fifth largest producer of wind power with 95% investment from private sector. Greater reliance on these offers economic, social, and environmental benefits.

nodes.label: Power/Electricity Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Most visible form of energy identified with progress. Demand growth exceeds GDP growth -- 8% GDP growth needs 12% power supply growth. In 2003-04: thermal 70%, hydro/wind 28%, nuclear 2.4%. India needs to add 1,00,000 MW between 2000-2012 but can only add 20,000 MW per year. Installed capacity is under-utilised.

nodes.label: Power Sector Challenges
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Five major challenges: (1) Insufficient installed capacity for 7% GDP growth, (2) State Electricity Boards losses exceeding Rs 500 billion from T&D losses, wrong pricing, inefficiency, electricity theft, (3) Private sector yet to play major role, (4) High power tariffs causing public unrest, (5) Thermal plants facing coal supply shortage.

nodes.label: Thermal Power
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Accounts for about 70% of India's power generation capacity (2003-04). Mainstay of India's power sector. Faces shortage of raw materials and coal supplies. Emits large quantities of CO2 (greenhouse gas) and produces fly ash which pollutes water and land if not properly managed.

nodes.label: Nuclear Energy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Only 2.4% of total primary energy consumption versus global average of 13% -- far too low. Has environmental advantages and likely economical in the long run. Important source of electric power that could help bridge the energy gap but its share in India's energy mix remains disproportionately small.

nodes.label: Transmission and Distribution Losses
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Electricity generated is not fully consumed by end-users. Part consumed by power station auxiliaries, part lost in transmission. What reaches homes/offices/factories is net availability. SEBs incur losses from T&D losses, free/subsidised power to farmers, and electricity theft. These are major reasons for the power sector's financial crisis.

nodes.label: Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Village-level health facilities generally manned by a single doctor, nurse, and limited medicines. ANM (Auxiliary Nursing Midwife) is the first provider of primary healthcare in rural areas. By 2000, 22,842 PHCs existed. But only 38% have required doctors and only 30% have sufficient medicine stock. Cannot even offer X-ray or blood tests in rural areas.

nodes.label: Private Health Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Over 70% of hospitals in India are private, controlling nearly two-fifths of beds. 60% of dispensaries are private. Serves 80% of out-patients and 46% of in-patients. Dominates medical education, diagnostics, pharmaceuticals. Over 13 lakh medical enterprises employing 22 lakh people (2001-02). Largely unregulated with some unregistered practitioners (quacks).

nodes.label: Urban-Rural Health Divide
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Though 70% of population is rural, only one-fifth of hospitals are there. Rural India has about half the dispensaries. Of 7 lakh beds, only 11% in rural areas. Only 0.36 hospitals per lakh rural people versus 3.6 in urban areas. Rural PHCs lack X-ray/blood testing. Rural health access without proper care rose from 15% (1986) to 24% (2003).

nodes.label: Medical Tourism
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Foreigners visiting India for cheaper medical services -- surgeries, transplants, dental, cosmetic care. In 2004-05, 1,50,000 foreigners visited for medical treatment, expected to grow 15% annually. By 2012, India could earn over 100 billion rupees. Driven by latest medical technologies, qualified professionals, and lower costs compared to home countries.

nodes.label: Health Expenditure in India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Only 4.8% of GDP on health (compared to China's 5.8%, USA's 14.6%). Government share of total health expenditure only 21.3%. Government health spending only 4.4% of total government spending. Poorest 20% spend 12% of their income on healthcare while the rich spend only 2%. Poor often sell land or pledge children to afford treatment.

nodes.label: Women's Health Issues
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Child sex ratio deteriorated from 945 (1991) to 927 (2001) indicating growing female foeticide. Close to 3,00,000 girls under 15 already borne children. Over 50% of married women aged 15-49 have anaemia. Iron deficiency contributed to 19% of maternal deaths. Abortions are a major cause of maternal morbidity and mortality.

nodes.label: Environment: Definition and Functions
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Total planetary inheritance and totality of all resources. Includes biotic (birds, animals, plants, forests, fisheries) and abiotic (air, water, land, rocks, sunlight) factors. Four vital functions: (1) supplies resources (renewable and non-renewable), (2) assimilates waste, (3) sustains life through genetic and bio-diversity, (4) provides aesthetic services.

nodes.label: Absorptive Capacity of Environment
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Ability of the environment to absorb degradation. When waste generation is within this capacity, no environmental crisis occurs. Population explosion and industrial revolution pushed demand beyond regeneration rates and waste beyond absorptive capacity, creating a supply-demand reversal for environmental quality.

nodes.label: Environmental Challenges in India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India's environment faces a dichotomy: poverty-induced degradation AND pollution from affluence/industrialisation. Priority issues: (1) land degradation, (2) biodiversity loss, (3) air pollution especially vehicular in cities, (4) freshwater management, (5) solid waste management. India has 16% of world's population on 2.5% of land, 20% of livestock.

nodes.label: Land Degradation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Caused by: deforestation, unsustainable fuel wood extraction, shifting cultivation, forest encroachment, overgrazing, inadequate soil conservation, improper crop rotation, indiscriminate use of agro-chemicals, improper irrigation. Per capita forestland only 0.08 hectare versus 0.47 requirement. Soil eroded at 5.3 billion tonnes per year, losing critical NPK nutrients.

nodes.label: Brundtland Commission
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Produced the seminal report 'Our Common Future' that defined sustainable development as meeting basic needs of all and extending opportunity for a better life. Emphasised moral obligation to hand over the planet in good order to future generations. Present generation should bequeath equal or better 'quality of life' assets.

nodes.label: Herman Daly's Sustainability Principles
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Leading environmental economist's framework: (1) Limit human population within carrying capacity (plimsoll line analogy), (2) Technological progress should be input-efficient not input-consuming, (3) Renewable resources extraction must not exceed regeneration rate, (4) Non-renewable depletion must not exceed rate of renewable substitutes creation, (5) Correct pollution inefficiencies.

nodes.label: Solar Power through Photovoltaic Cells
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India has large natural endowment of solar energy. Photovoltaic cells capture solar energy and convert it to electricity using special materials. Extremely useful for remote areas where grid power supply is impossible or costly. Totally pollution-free technology. Thane Municipal Corporation made solar water heating compulsory for new buildings.

nodes.label: Wind Power
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: In high wind-speed areas, wind turbines generate electricity without adverse environmental impact. India is already the world's fifth largest producer of wind power with over 95% investment from private sector. Initial cost is high but benefits are substantial. No carbon emissions, no fossil fuel dependency.

nodes.label: LPG and Gobar Gas in Rural Areas
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Rural households using wood/dung cake cause deforestation, green cover reduction, cattle dung wastage, and air pollution. Subsidised LPG provided as clean fuel reducing household pollution. Gobar gas plants use cattle dung to produce gas as fuel, with slurry remaining as organic fertiliser and soil conditioner. Provided through easy loans and subsidy.

nodes.label: Biocomposting
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India nearly abandoned compost in favour of chemical fertilisers in the last five decades, adversely affecting productive land, water bodies, ground water, and increasing irrigation demand. Farmers are returning to organic compost. Earthworm-based vermicomposting speeds up the process. Also reduces civic waste disposal burden.

nodes.label: Biopest Control
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Green revolution led to excessive chemical pesticide use contaminating food, soil, water, ground water, and even milk, meat, and fish. Plant-based alternatives include neem-derived pest controlling chemicals. Mixed cropping and crop rotation help. Natural predators (snakes for rats, owls/peacocks for pests, lizards) also provide biological pest control.

nodes.label: Traditional Knowledge and Practices
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Indian people traditionally lived as part of the environment, not its controller. Traditional agriculture, healthcare (Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan, folk systems), housing, transport were all environment-friendly. India has about 15,000 plant species with medicinal properties, 8,000 in regular use. Return to traditional systems is a sustainable development strategy.

nodes.label: Human Development Indicators Comparison
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: China outperforms India and Pakistan on most human development indicators: life expectancy, literacy rates, infant mortality, maternal mortality, access to sanitation. India has higher literacy than Pakistan but lower than China. All three face challenges in gender equity. HDI rankings reflect these disparities.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: State Owned Enterprises (SOEs) in China
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Equivalent of India's public sector enterprises. During reforms, SOEs were made to face competition from private sector firms and township/village enterprises. This stands in contrast to India where public sector enterprises were given monopoly status in many sectors until 1991 reforms.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: National Income
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Net National Product at factor cost. Represents GNP at market prices minus depreciation minus indirect taxes plus subsidies. It is the sum of all factor incomes (rent + wages + interest + profit) earned by nationals. The most appropriate measure for comparing living standards is per capita real national income.

nodes.label: Market Price vs Factor Cost
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Market price includes indirect taxes and excludes subsidies. Factor cost excludes indirect taxes and includes subsidies. FC = MP - Indirect Taxes + Subsidies. National Income is measured at factor cost; GDP is commonly reported at market price. The difference matters for accurate income measurement.

nodes.label: Three Methods of Measuring National Income
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: National income can be measured by: (1) Production/Value Added method -- sum of value added at each stage, (2) Income method -- sum of all factor incomes (rent + wages + interest + profit), (3) Expenditure method -- sum of final expenditures (C + I + G + X - M). All three give the same result.

nodes.label: Value Added Method
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Measures GDP by summing the value added at each stage of production across all sectors. Value added = Value of output - Value of intermediate consumption. Avoids double counting by counting only the value added by each firm, not the full value of output.

nodes.label: Double Counting Problem
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The error of counting the value of intermediate goods more than once in GDP calculation. Avoided by either using the value added method (counting only value added at each stage) or by counting only final goods and services. Intermediate goods used up entirely in production are excluded.

nodes.label: Final vs Intermediate Goods
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Final goods are purchased for final consumption or investment, not for resale or further production. Intermediate goods are used as inputs in production of other goods. Only final goods are counted in GDP to avoid double counting. The same good can be final or intermediate depending on its use.

nodes.label: Expenditure Method
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Measures GDP by summing all final expenditures: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). C is private consumption expenditure, I is gross domestic capital formation (investment), G is government consumption expenditure, (X-M) is net exports. This is the most commonly used formula for GDP.

nodes.label: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A method of comparing living standards between countries by adjusting for differences in price levels. PPP exchange rates equalize the purchasing power of different currencies by comparing the prices of the same basket of goods across countries. India's economy is much larger in PPP terms than at market exchange rates.

nodes.label: High Powered Money (H)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Also called Reserve Money or Monetary Base. H = Currency in circulation (with public) + Reserves of commercial banks (with RBI). It is the money produced by RBI and the government. Total money supply is a multiple of H. Changes in H cause multiplied changes in money supply.

nodes.label: Money Multiplier
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The ratio of money supply to high powered money. Money Multiplier = 1/r where r is the reserve ratio. The multiplier increases when: banking habit increases (more deposits), CRR decreases, or currency-deposit ratio falls. It decreases when CRR or SLR increase, or when public holds more cash.

nodes.label: Commercial Banks
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Financial institutions that accept deposits from the public and make loans. They create credit through the process of accepting deposits and making loans. Primary functions: accepting deposits (demand, savings, fixed), lending, and creating credit. Scheduled commercial banks are regulated by RBI.

nodes.label: Credit Creation by Commercial Banks
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The process by which banks create money beyond the initial deposit through successive rounds of lending. When a bank receives a deposit, it keeps a fraction as reserve (CRR) and lends the rest. The loan creates a new deposit in the banking system. Total credit created = Initial Deposit x (1/CRR).

nodes.label: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The percentage of total deposits that commercial banks must maintain as cash reserves with the RBI. A quantitative tool of monetary policy. Increasing CRR reduces lendable funds and contracts money supply; decreasing CRR expands money supply. Directly affects money multiplier.

nodes.label: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The percentage of net demand and time liabilities that banks must maintain in the form of liquid assets (cash, gold, approved government securities). Reducing SLR frees up more funds for lending and may lead banks to cut lending rates. Ensures solvency of banks.

nodes.label: Repo Rate
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The interest rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities. A key policy rate used to control inflation and money supply. Increasing repo rate makes borrowing costlier for banks, reducing lending and money supply. It is the main instrument of monetary policy under the LAF framework.

nodes.label: Reverse Repo Rate
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The interest rate at which RBI borrows funds from commercial banks. When RBI wants to absorb excess liquidity, it increases the reverse repo rate, incentivizing banks to park funds with RBI instead of lending. Always lower than the repo rate.

nodes.label: Open Market Operations (OMO)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The buying and selling of government securities by RBI in the open market. When RBI buys securities, it injects money into the economy (expansionary). When RBI sells securities, it absorbs money (contractionary). A quantitative instrument of monetary policy. Also used in sterilization operations.

nodes.label: Monetary Policy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Policy by which RBI controls money supply and credit conditions to achieve macroeconomic objectives -- primarily price stability. Instruments include CRR, SLR, Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, Bank Rate, OMO, and MSF. Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a 6-member body chaired by RBI Governor, decides the repo rate.

nodes.label: Time Deposits (Fixed Deposits)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Bank deposits held for a fixed period and not withdrawable on demand without penalty. Included in M3 (Broad Money) but not in M1 (Narrow Money). Earn higher interest than demand deposits. They represent less liquid money that adds to the broader money supply.

nodes.label: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A 6-member statutory body that decides the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target. Constituted under RBI Act (amended 2016). 3 members from RBI (including Governor as chairman) and 3 external members appointed by the Central Government. Decisions by majority vote; Governor has casting vote.

nodes.label: Government Budget
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An annual financial statement of the government's estimated receipts and expenditure for the fiscal year. Presented by the Finance Minister before Parliament (Article 112). Prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance. Serves as an instrument of fiscal policy for economic stabilization, redistribution, and resource allocation.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Revenue Receipts
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Receipts that neither create any liability nor reduce the assets of the government. Two types: (1) Tax revenue -- income tax, corporation tax, customs, excise, GST, etc., (2) Non-tax revenue -- profits of PSUs, interest on loans, fees, fines, dividends, grants from foreign governments. They are recurring in nature.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Capital Receipts
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Receipts that either create a liability or reduce assets of the government. Include: borrowings (create liability), recovery of loans given (reduce assets), and disinvestment proceeds (reduce assets). Interest received on loans is NOT a capital receipt -- it is revenue receipt as it doesn't reduce the loan asset.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Revenue Expenditure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Expenditure that neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities. Includes salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, defence expenditure (except capital items), and grants to states/UTs. All non-plan expenditure items (defence, interest, subsidies, pensions) are revenue expenditure.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Capital Expenditure
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Expenditure that creates assets or reduces liabilities. Includes expenditure on roads, buildings, machinery (asset creation), and repayment of loans (liability reduction). Loans and advances to states/UTs are also capital expenditure. Capital expenditure contributes to productive capacity.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Fiscal Deficit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts). It indicates the total borrowing requirement of the government. Financed by borrowings from RBI (monetization), market borrowings, and external borrowings. FRBMA targets reduction of fiscal deficit.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Revenue Deficit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Indicates that the government's regular income is insufficient to meet its regular expenditure. A revenue deficit means the government is borrowing to finance consumption expenditure, which is considered undesirable as it adds to debt without creating assets.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Primary Deficit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments. Indicates the borrowing requirement excluding interest obligations on past debt. A zero primary deficit means the government is borrowing only to pay interest on existing debt, not for new expenditure.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Direct Taxes
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Taxes where the liability and incidence fall on the same person -- cannot be shifted. Include income tax, corporation tax (levied and kept exclusively by Union), wealth tax (abolished 2015), and capital gains tax. Corporation tax is the largest single source of Union tax revenue.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Indirect Taxes
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Taxes where the incidence can be shifted from the person who pays to the final consumer. Include GST (replaced excise, service tax, VAT), customs duty. Service tax was an indirect tax levied by the Central Government. Indirect taxes are regressive -- same rate for rich and poor.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Progressive Taxation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A tax system where the tax rate increases as the taxable income increases. Higher-income earners pay a larger percentage. India's income tax is progressive with slabs. Progressive taxation combined with progressive expenditure is the best method for redistribution of income.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Fiscal Policy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Government's use of taxation and expenditure to influence the economy. Expansionary fiscal policy (more spending, less tax) combats recession. Contractionary fiscal policy (less spending, more tax) controls inflation. Tools include government spending, tax rates, subsidies, and public borrowing.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Deficit Financing
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Government borrowing to finance the gap between expenditure and revenue. In India, deficit financing is used for economic development. Sources include market borrowings, RBI borrowing (most inflationary), external borrowing, and small savings. Excessive deficit financing can lead to inflation.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Consolidated Fund of India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The fund into which all revenues received by the government, all loans raised, and all money received in repayment of loans are credited. No money can be withdrawn from it without Parliament's authorization. Established under Article 266(1) of the Constitution. Salaries of judges and CAG are charged on it.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Contingency Fund of India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A fund at the disposal of the President of India to meet unforeseen expenditure pending authorization by Parliament. Established under Article 267. After expenditure is authorized by Parliament, the fund is recouped. Each state also has a Contingency Fund at the disposal of the Governor.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Public Account of India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Account for money received by the government which does not belong to it -- flows in and out. Includes provident fund deposits, small savings, court deposits. Disbursements from the Public Account do NOT need Parliamentary authorization (unlike Consolidated Fund). Established under Article 266(2).
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Subsidies
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Financial assistance by the government to reduce the cost of goods and services for consumers or producers. Major subsidies: food (through PDS), fertilizer, and petroleum. Subsidies are revenue expenditure. Rationalizing subsidies is a key measure to reduce fiscal deficit. Food subsidy is the largest among the three.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Interest Payments
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The single largest component of non-plan revenue expenditure of the Union Government. Interest payments on past borrowings eat into current revenues and constrain fiscal space. High borrowing keeps real interest rates elevated, crowding out private investment. Fiscal deficit minus interest payments gives primary deficit.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Vote on Account / Interim Budget
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A vote on account deals only with the expenditure side of the budget, used by a regular government to get Parliament's approval for expenditure until the full budget is passed. An interim budget includes both expenditure and receipts. When the annual budget is not passed, the Prime Minister submits the resignation of the Council of Ministers.
nodes.chapter_title: The Government Budget and the Economy

nodes.label: Capital Account
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Records all international capital transactions -- purchases and sales of assets between residents and non-residents. Includes FDI, FPI (portfolio investment), external commercial borrowings (ECBs), NRI deposits, and changes in foreign exchange reserves. A capital account surplus finances a current account deficit.

nodes.label: Exchange Rate
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The price of one currency in terms of another. Two types: nominal exchange rate (simple price ratio) and real exchange rate (adjusted for price level differences). Determined by demand and supply of foreign exchange. Increase in NEER indicates appreciation of rupee.

nodes.label: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Investment by a foreign entity in productive assets of another country with a lasting interest and significant influence (typically 10% or more equity). Most stable form of foreign capital inflow -- better than portfolio investment or commercial loans for host country. Recorded in the capital account of BoP.

nodes.label: Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Investment by foreign entities in financial assets (shares, bonds, etc.) without controlling interest. More volatile than FDI -- often called 'hot money' as it can flow out quickly during crises. Recorded in the capital account. Tight monetary policy in the US (like Fed rate hikes) can lead to FPI outflow from India (capital flight).

nodes.label: Current Account Deficit (CAD)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: When the current account shows a deficit, meaning the country's imports of goods, services, and transfers exceed its exports. India typically runs a CAD. Financed by capital account surplus (FDI, FPI, ECBs). High CAD can lead to a BoP crisis if capital inflows dry up.

nodes.label: Currency Convertibility
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The ability to freely convert domestic currency to foreign currencies. Current account convertibility: India allows free conversion for trade and service transactions (achieved 1994). Capital account convertibility: free conversion for investment and lending -- India has only partial capital account convertibility.

nodes.label: Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: NEER adjusted for relative price levels between domestic and foreign countries. An increase in REER does NOT indicate improvement in trade competitiveness (it means real appreciation). If domestic inflation rises faster than trading partners', NEER and REER diverge -- REER rises more, indicating loss of competitiveness.

nodes.label: Labour (Factor of Production)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Most abundant factor of production in India. Includes both skilled and manual workers. Farm labourers are paid wages (cash or kind) and often earn below the government-set minimum wage due to intense competition for work.

nodes.label: Farm Labourers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Workers from landless families or small plot cultivators who work for wages on others' land. Have no right over crops grown. Government minimum wage was Rs 300/day (2017) but actual wages often lower. Among the poorest in villages.

nodes.label: Unequal Land Distribution
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: About one-third of farming families in India are landless. 80% of total farmers are small farmers cultivating less than 2 hectares. 60 medium/large farmer families in Palampur owned more than half the village land. Reflects structural inequality.

nodes.label: Calorie Requirement
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Accepted average calorie intake for determining poverty line: 2400 calories/person/day in rural areas and 2100 in urban areas. Rural requirement is higher due to more physical work. Monetary expenditure for these calories is revised periodically.

nodes.label: Tendulkar Committee Methodology
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Methodology for poverty estimation adopted in India. Poverty ratio declined from 45% (1993-94) to 37.2% (2004-05) to 22% (2011-12). Number of poor declined from 407 million (2004-05) to 270 million (2011-12) with average annual decline of 2.2 percentage points.

nodes.label: Vulnerable Groups to Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Most vulnerable: Scheduled Castes (29% poor), Scheduled Tribes (43% poor), rural agricultural labourers, and urban casual labourers (34% poor). Women, elderly, and female infants face intra-household inequality. Double disadvantage for SC/ST landless casual workers.

nodes.label: Social Exclusion
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Process through which individuals or groups are excluded from facilities, benefits, and opportunities. Both a cause and consequence of poverty. Example: caste system excluding certain castes from equal opportunities. Can cause more damage than low income alone.

nodes.label: Vulnerability to Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Measures the probability of certain communities or individuals becoming or remaining poor. Determined by available options for alternative living -- assets, education, health, job opportunities. Includes risk from natural disasters and social/economic ability to handle them.

nodes.label: Inter-State Poverty Disparities
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Bihar (33.7%) and Orissa (32.6%) are poorest states. Significant decline in Kerala, Maharashtra, AP, TN, Gujarat, West Bengal. Punjab/Haryana: reduced poverty via agricultural growth. Kerala: human resource development. West Bengal: land reforms. AP/TN: PDS effectiveness.

nodes.label: Global Poverty Trends
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: World Bank defines extreme poverty as living on less than $1.90/day (2011 PPP). Global poverty fell from 35% (1990) to 10.68% (2013). China: 88.3% (1981) to 1.9% (2013). Sub-Saharan Africa: rose from 54% to 41%. South Asia declined from 54% to 15%. UN SDG: end poverty by 2030.

nodes.label: Human Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Broader concept beyond income-based poverty. Includes lack of education, shelter, healthcare, job security, self-confidence, and freedom from caste/gender discrimination. Definition of poverty changes with development -- eradication is a moving target.

nodes.label: Anti-Poverty Strategy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Two-pronged approach: (1) promotion of economic growth and (2) targeted anti-poverty programmes. Growth rate jumped from 3.5%/year (1970s) to 6% (1980s-90s). Strong link between economic growth and poverty reduction, but poor may not directly benefit without targeted programmes.

nodes.label: Food Availability
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Domestic food production + food imports + previous years' government stock. India achieved self-sufficiency in foodgrains through Green Revolution. Total foodgrain production was 252.22 million tonnes in 2015-16. UP and MP were largest producers.

nodes.label: Food Insecure Groups
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Worst affected: landless people, traditional artisans, petty self-employed, destitutes. Urban: ill-paid occupations, casual labour. Social: SCs, STs, lower OBCs. Regions: eastern UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh. Women and children under 5 especially vulnerable.

nodes.label: Buffer Stock
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Stock of foodgrains (wheat and rice) procured by government through FCI. Purchased at Minimum Support Price (MSP) from surplus-producing states. Distributed in deficit areas at Issue Price (lower than market price). Used to resolve shortages during calamities.

nodes.label: Food Corporation of India (FCI)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Central government agency that purchases wheat and rice from farmers at MSP, stores in granaries, and distributes through PDS. In 2014, stock was 65.3 million tonnes -- much above buffer norms. Faces criticism for high carrying costs, wastage, and grain deterioration.

nodes.label: Minimum Support Price (MSP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Pre-announced price at which government purchases foodgrains from farmers. Declared every year before sowing season to incentivise production. Rising MSP has increased procurement costs. Procurement concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, Western UP, and AP -- mainly for wheat and rice.

nodes.label: Issue Price
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Price at which government-procured foodgrains are sold to consumers through PDS, lower than market price. Different issue prices for different categories: AAY gets lowest price (Rs 2/kg wheat, Rs 3/kg rice), BPL and APL get progressively higher prices.

nodes.label: Targeted PDS (TPDS)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Introduced June 1997 to target the poor in all areas with differential pricing. First time a different price policy was adopted for poor (BPL) and non-poor (APL). Three types of ration cards: Antyodaya (poorest), BPL (below poverty line), APL (above poverty line).

nodes.label: PDS Criticism and Challenges
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Dealer malpractices: diverting grains to open market, selling poor quality, irregular opening. FCI godowns overflowing while hunger persists. Rising MSP increases procurement costs. Concentrated procurement in few regions distorts cropping patterns. APL prices near market rates reduce incentive.

nodes.label: Subsidy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Payment by government to a producer to supplement the market price of a commodity. Keeps consumer prices low while maintaining higher income for domestic producers. Food subsidy covers the difference between procurement cost (MSP + handling) and issue price.
